subject: Appropriate use of multiple comparison adjustment following advanced.procD.lm()

messages.author: a6eb4e0031b55437
messages.subject: Appropriate use of multiple comparison adjustment following advanced.procD.lm()
parts:
Dear geomorph community,

I'm comparing static allometric slopes of 38 species using advanced.procD.lm() and analyzing the pairwise p-values given by $P.slopes.dist. I know from a previous post on this site that the test itself does not perform a multiple comparisons adjustment and that it is a user-based decision on what to do afterwards. 

However, I have noticed that recent literature has not performed any adjustments on similarly large datasets. For example Esquerré et al (2017) has 40 species of pythons and while they use an adjustment for their heterochrony test, they don't use an adjustment on their advanced.procD.lm() pairwise analysis of slopes. In their Methods, they state that the "Statistical significance [of the pairwise slopes test] was evaluated with a residual randomization permutation procedure with 10,000 iterations." 

Is the permutation procedure alone sufficient? Looking at Adams and Collyer (2009) on comparing phenotypic trajectories (with my imperfect stats knowledge), I found this statement about the permutation procedure: "By performing many iterations, an empirical null distribution of a test statistic for the SSCP (sum of squares and cross-products) is created, and the significance of the observed statistic is inferred from its percentile in the null distribution."

Does this mean that no multiple comparison adjustment is needed because essentially the statistics (the p-values) come from one test? 

Many thanks in advance for any advice or clarifications. 

Best,
Ariel
Ariel E Marcy | PhD Candidate in Evolutionary Biology at The University of Queensland

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Appropriate use of multiple comparison adjustment following advanced.procD.lm()
parts:
Ariel,

I would not over-interpret that quote as advocacy to disregard pairwise adjustments of alpha.  P-values for statistics are almost always estimated.  In parametric statistics, a theoretical probability distribution - like an F-, or t-distribution - might be used.  In geomorph, we generally use RRPP to generate empirical distributions.  The percentile of a statistic in the distribution is the estimate of the P-value (use fewer permutations and this estimate might be biased, if the true value is far lower than the number of permutations will allow to be estimated accurately).

You might be thinking of posthoc tests that adjust P-values.  This is one approach; the other is to adjust alpha.  Either way, one is attempting to ascertain the “significance” based on the established criterion.  In geomorph, we do not adjust the P-values but the user is free to adjust their pairwise alpha levels.  Inferring significance from the percentile of a statistic in its sampling (null) distribution (P-value), as stated, indicates nothing about what the alpha level should be.  That is the user’s choice.  A P-value of 0.03 might be “significant” for the user who does not adjust alpha levels but not significant for the user that does.  Nevertheless, 0.03 means that 3% of the time, the statistic was equalled or exceeded in random permutations.  Knowing this, one can infer the significance based on their own interpretation of whether 3% is low or high.

Cheers!
Mike
